Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Vignette:
Kwame remembered the intersection first, the way the wet asphalt caught the streetlights like scattered glass, then the shriek of tires that belonged to the truck crossing his line. He had been driving his sedan after a late rehearsal at the community center, his body still loose from hours of choreography, when the impact threw him hard against the driver’s side door. The window fractured into a million white sparks. He was pinned, his ribs pressing against the steering column, and for a long time there was only the hiss of the radiator and the rhythmic thump of his own pulse in his ears. Help came eventually, but not quickly enough to quiet the frantic tightening in his chest. He watched the headlights of the first responders sweep past twice before they finally stopped. The officers who arrived later asked him to sit in the back of the cruiser while they filled out paperwork, and the long, silent wait convinced him that the systems designed to keep people safe had simply missed him when it mattered. In the weeks that followed, Kwame tried to lay the event out on paper for his primary care doctor, but the details refused to align. He knew there had been a moment of weightlessness, a flash of blue, a smell of burnt rubber, yet the pieces would not stitch into a line. Whenever he forced himself to reach backward into the hours before the collision, his mind simply went quiet, as if a switch had been thrown. He stopped telling anyone about it, not because he did not want to, but because trying to reconstruct it only left him feeling unmoored. What settled in instead was a quiet certainty that his own judgment had failed him. He could not trust that he would navigate correctly again, and he certainly could not trust the fragile architecture of his legs and hips. At sixty-eight, his body had been his livelihood, the instrument through which he taught classical and contemporary dance to young adults; now it felt like a unreliable companion that might buckle without warning. After his wife Eleanor passed two years prior, the quiet of his home had always been heavy, but now it felt like a cage. The world outside his apartment began to feel like a sequence of untrustworthy delays. He would sit at the kitchen table and check his watch if a package tracker showed no movement, his breath shallowing until the expected event finally occurred. On the street, a dropped toolbox from a construction site or a car backfiring made him jump, his shoulders locking before he could tell himself it was nothing. Inside his own home, he moved his armchair until its back rested flush against the brick wall behind it, only then allowing his muscles to ease. Friends from his old dance circle called and texted, inviting him to gallery openings and Sunday suppers, but he let the messages accumulate. Seeing them felt like being pulled back into a room where he no longer belonged, so he stopped answering. He stood in the doorway of his own studio, the hardwood floor scarred by decades of pivot turns, and listened to the distant siren wail down the block. The sound made his shoulders lock, and he stepped back, closing the door without going in. When he finally saw a clinician, he told her he would rather not talk about the crash itself, and for the next several sessions he changed the subject whenever the conversation drifted toward it, preferring to sit with silence than risk the unraveling he feared. The avoidance had quietly rewritten his days. He no longer went to the rehearsal space he had rented for thirty years. When he finally tried to walk to the grocery store three months after the accident, he found himself circling the block twice before turning back, his steps heavy and unsure. The studio mirrors still stood in the corner of his living room, gathering dust, and each time he passed them he felt a fresh wave of doubt about whether his joints would hold. What finally brought him back to the clinic was a Tuesday afternoon when he realized he had not left his apartment in four days, and the quiet of the rooms was louder than any siren. He told the intake coordinator that he wanted to remember who he was before the intersection, not so he could relive the crash, but because he was tired of waiting for his body to betray him again. He did not know if walking again would ever feel safe, but he hoped someone could help him stop bracing for the next delay, the next sound, the next failure of care.
